blocks.text: A Sparse Table is a data structure built for one very specific situation: an array that never changes, where you need to repeatedly answer range queries such as the minimum, maximum, or gcd of a subarray, and you want each query answered as fast as physically possible.
After an O(n log n) preprocessing step, a Sparse Table answers every range query in O(1) time, regardless of how large the range is.

That O(1) query time is the entire reason this structure exists, and it comes at a price that has to be stated clearly up front: a Sparse Table cannot be updated. Once it is built, the underlying array is frozen. If a single element changes, the whole table must be rebuilt from scratch.
This is a deliberate trade. Compare the three structures you would reach for when a problem asks for range queries:

items: Sparse Table: no updates at all, but O(1) query time
Fenwick Tree: supports point updates, but only O(log n) query time
Segment Tree: supports updates and even range updates, but also only O(log n) query time

blocks.text: If the input is truly static and you only care about squeezing the query time down as far as it will go, a Sparse Table wins outright. The moment the array needs to change even once, it is the wrong tool, and a Fenwick Tree or Segment Tree takes over.

The second condition that makes a Sparse Table work is that the operation being queried must be idempotent (applying it again to overlapping data does not change the result). Minimum, maximum, and gcd are idempotent. Sum is not, and that single distinction is worth a very close look before writing any code, because it decides whether this structure even applies to a given problem.

The single most important fact about a Sparse Table is that it is built for arrays that never change. Not rarely change, never change. There is no update operation, no partial rebuild, no clever trick to patch one value in. If the array changes, the table is stale and every query result built from it becomes wrong.

This is not a limitation to work around, it is the whole design. By giving up update support entirely, a Sparse Table is free to precompute an answer for every possible power of two range once, up front, and then answer any query by combining just two of those precomputed answers, no matter how large the range is. That is what makes O(1) query time possible.
It helps to line the three structures up side by side and see exactly where each one sits:

blocks.content: {"headers":["Structure","Update","Query","Best for"],"rows":[["Sparse Table","Not supported","O(1)","Static array, idempotent range queries (min, max, gcd)"],["Fenwick Tree","O(log n)","O(log n)","Frequent point updates with sum, xor, or count queries"],["Segment Tree","O(log n)","O(log n)","Updates plus min, max, or more complex range operations"]]}

blocks.text: If the array is genuinely static and the operation is idempotent, a Sparse Table gives the fastest possible query time, a real O(1), full stop. That is the single tradeoff to remember: static array and idempotent operation in exchange for O(1) queries.
An operation is idempotent when applying it again to data it has already been applied to does not change the answer. Formally, combining a value with itself gives back that same value.

This property matters because the whole Sparse Table query trick works by combining two precomputed ranges that overlap in the middle. For an idempotent operation, counting the overlapping part twice changes nothing, so the combined answer is still correct.

blocks.caption: Overlap is harmless for min, max, and gcd, but silently corrupts a sum
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762808-11663898.png
A concrete example makes this obvious. Take the array [4, 2, 7, 1, 5, 3] and suppose two overlapping precomputed ranges both happen to include the value at index 3, which holds 1.

codes.javascript:
array:   [4, 2, 7, 1, 5, 3]
index:     0  1  2  3  4  5

Two overlapping ranges, both covering index 3:
  Left  range [1, 4] -> values 2, 7, 1, 5 -> min = 1
  Right range [3, 5] -> values 1, 5, 3     -> min = 1

Combining with min:
  min(1, 1) = 1        // correct, overlap changes nothing

Now compare with sum:
  Left  range [1, 4] sum = 2 + 7 + 1 + 5 = 15
  Right range [3, 5] sum = 1 + 5 + 3     = 9

Combining with sum:
  sum(15, 9) = 24       // WRONG, the value 1 at index 3
                        // and the value 5 at index 4 were
                        // both counted twice

blocks.text: The min query gives the right answer no matter how much the two ranges overlap, because taking the minimum of the same value twice is still that value. The sum query does not, because every element that falls inside the overlapping middle gets added in twice.

This is exactly why a Sparse Table works beautifully for min, max, gcd, and bitwise and, but cannot correctly answer sum queries without extra bookkeeping to avoid double counting the overlap, at which point the O(1) query trick stops applying. For range sum on a static array, a plain prefix sum array is the simpler and correct choice.

content.title: 3. The Core Idea: Precomputing Power of Two Ranges

blocks.text: Instead of precomputing an answer for every possible range, which would take O(n^2) space, a Sparse Table only precomputes answers for ranges whose length is a power of two.
Define sparse[k][i] as the answer (say, the minimum) for the range that starts at index i and has length exactly 2^k.

codes.javascript:
sparse[0][i] = arr[i]                          // length 1 range, base case
sparse[k][i] = combine(sparse[k-1][i], sparse[k-1][i + 2^(k-1)])

blocks.text: The recurrence is the entire idea in one line: a range of length 2^k is just two adjacent ranges of length 2^(k-1) placed next to each other, so its answer is simply the combined answer of those two halves.

blocks.caption: Each level doubles the range length by combining two half length ranges from the level below
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762808-795354549.png
blocks.alt: The Core Idea: Precomputing Power of Two Ranges

blocks.text: How many levels are needed?
Since the range length doubles at every level, the largest useful value of k is around log2(n). Beyond that point, a range of length 2^k would no longer fit inside an array of size n.

That gives roughly log2(n) levels, each holding up to n entries, for a total table size of O(n log n) cells. Filling every cell using the recurrence above also takes O(n log n) time, since each cell is filled with a single combine call.

content.title: 4. Answering Any Range Query in O(1)

blocks.text: The table only stores answers for power of two length ranges, so answering an arbitrary query [l, r] needs one more idea: pick the largest power of two that still fits inside the query length, and use it twice.

codes.javascript:
length = r - l + 1
k = floor(log2(length))          // largest power of two that fits

leftBlock  = sparse[k][l]              // covers [l, l + 2^k - 1]
rightBlock = sparse[k][r - 2^k + 1]    // covers [r - 2^k + 1, r]

answer = combine(leftBlock, rightBlock)

blocks.text: The left block starts exactly at l and the right block ends exactly at r, so together the two blocks are guaranteed to cover every index in [l, r]. If the query length is not itself a power of two, these two blocks will overlap somewhere in the middle.

blocks.caption: The left and right blocks together cover the whole query range and may overlap in the middle
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762809-408286528.png
blocks.alt: Answering Any Range Query in O1

blocks.text: Why the overlap is not a problem

This overlap is exactly the situation covered earlier: because min, max, and gcd are idempotent, counting the middle portion in both blocks does not change the combined answer. The two lookups plus one combine call all run in constant time, which is what makes the whole query O(1).

The core clever idea of the entire structure is this: cover the query with two overlapping precomputed blocks instead of one exact block. Idempotence is what makes that overlap free, and that is the only reason O(1) queries are possible at all.

content.title: 5. Building the Sparse Table in C++

blocks.text: Computing floor(log2(length)) for every query is worth doing efficiently. The simplest approach precomputes a small log table once. A faster alternative on modern compilers is the built in __lg or __builtin_clz, which compute it directly from the bit representation of an integer.

With the log table ready, building the Sparse Table itself is a nested loop: the outer loop walks through each level k, and the inner loop fills every valid starting index i at that level using the two half length ranges from the previous level.
Building the whole table costs O(n log n) time and O(n log n) space, and it only needs to be done once, since the array is never going to change afterward.

The query function is a direct translation of the two overlapping block idea from the previous section: find the largest power of two that fits inside the range, then combine the block starting at l with the block ending at r.

Both array lookups and the single min call are constant time work, so the whole query runs in O(1) regardless of how wide the range [l, r] is. Whether the range covers 3 elements or 3 million, the query does the exact same fixed amount of work.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Structure","Preprocessing","Space","Query","Update"],"rows":[["Sparse Table","O(n log n)","O(n log n)","O(1)","Not supported"],["Fenwick Tree","O(n log n)","O(n)","O(log n)","O(log n)"],["Segment Tree","O(n)","O(n)","O(log n)","O(log n)"]]}

blocks.text: The row that matters most is the last column. A Sparse Table simply has nothing there, updates are not part of its design at all, not slow, not expensive, genuinely unsupported. Any problem that mutates the array even once needs a Fenwick Tree or Segment Tree instead.

Remember the shape of this tradeoff: Sparse Table spends a bit more space than a Fenwick Tree, in exchange for turning every query into a true O(1) lookup, but only for a frozen array and an idempotent operation.
Take the small array [5, 2, 6, 1, 8, 4] with 6 elements, indexed 0 through 5, and build the Sparse Table for range minimum.

codes.javascript:
array:   [5, 2, 6, 1, 8, 4]
index:     0  1  2  3  4  5

Level k = 0 (length 1), sparse[0][i] = arr[i]:
  sparse[0] = [5, 2, 6, 1, 8, 4]

Level k = 1 (length 2), sparse[1][i] = min(arr[i], arr[i+1]):
  sparse[1][0] = min(5, 2) = 2
  sparse[1][1] = min(2, 6) = 2
  sparse[1][2] = min(6, 1) = 1
  sparse[1][3] = min(1, 8) = 1
  sparse[1][4] = min(8, 4) = 4
  sparse[1] = [2, 2, 1, 1, 4]

Level k = 2 (length 4), sparse[2][i] = min(sparse[1][i], sparse[1][i+2]):
  sparse[2][0] = min(2, 1) = 1     // covers [0, 3]
  sparse[2][1] = min(2, 1) = 1     // covers [1, 4]
  sparse[2][2] = min(1, 4) = 1     // covers [2, 5]
  sparse[2] = [1, 1, 1]

blocks.text: Now trace a query for the range [1, 5], which has 5 elements, values 2, 6, 1, 8, 4. The largest power of two that fits inside a length of 5 is 4, so k = 2.

blocks.caption: Two overlapping length four blocks together cover the length five query range
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762809-53869567.png

codes.javascript:
l = 1, r = 5, length = 5, k = 2

leftBlock  = sparse[2][1] = 1      // covers indices [1, 4]
rightBlock = sparse[2][2] = 1      // covers indices [2, 5]

answer = min(leftBlock, rightBlock) = min(1, 1) = 1

blocks.text: The two blocks overlap at indices 2, 3, and 4, and index 3 (the value 1, the true minimum of the whole range) gets counted in both blocks. Because min is idempotent, that overlap costs nothing, the combined answer of 1 is exactly correct, and it was computed with a single comparison instead of scanning all 5 elements.
Range Minimum Query (RMQ)

This is the classic, textbook use case for a Sparse Table, and it is exactly what was built and traced above. Range Maximum Query is the mirror image, swap every min for a max and nothing else changes.
Range GCD Query
Greatest common divisor is idempotent (gcd(a, a) = a), so it slots into the exact same table and query logic, only the combine function changes.
Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) in O(1)

A less obvious but well known application: running an Euler tour over a tree turns the LCA problem into a range minimum query over the depths visited during the tour. Building a Sparse Table on top of that tour array answers any LCA query in O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing. That combination is a topic of its own and is not implemented in depth here, it is worth knowing this connection exists.

items: Medium Range Minimum Query style problems: given a fixed array and many range min or max queries, the canonical Sparse Table use case
Easy Range Sum Query, Immutable (LC 303): the array is static but the operation is sum, not min or max, so a plain prefix sum array is the correct and simpler tool here, not a Sparse Table
Hard Sliding Window Maximum (LC 239): a related but genuinely different problem, the window moves so nothing is static, this is usually solved with a monotonic deque rather than a Sparse Table

Using a Sparse Table for sum queries the two precomputed blocks overlap, and since sum is not idempotent, that overlapping middle portion gets added in twice, silently producing a wrong, inflated answer. Use a prefix sum array for static sum queries instead.

Forgetting that the array is static and trying to add an update method a Sparse Table has no update path at all, changing even one element invalidates the entire table and requires a full O(n log n) rebuild.

Off by one errors picking k the largest power of two that fits must satisfy 2^k <= length, and forgetting the offset used to align the right block's starting index is a very common source of subtle wrong answers.
Can you state, in one sentence, the exact tradeoff a Sparse Table makes (no updates, in exchange for O(1) queries)?
Can you explain why idempotence is required, and why sum queries break under the overlapping range trick?
Can you build the table from scratch, including the recurrence for sparse[k][i], in a few minutes?
Can you write the O(1) query, including correctly picking the largest power of two that fits the range length?
Do you know when to reach for Sparse Table versus Fenwick Tree versus Segment Tree versus plain prefix sum?
Can you name at least one problem, such as LCA via Euler tour, where Sparse Table is combined with another technique?
